newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire ethnic warfare flares as U.N. envoy arrives.
newsitem.headline: Zaire ethnic warfare flares as U.N. envoy arrives.

text.p: Ethnic warfare intensified in eastern Zaire on Sunday as a U.N. envoy arrived to seek ways of checking the spread of the conflict in the volatile region.
Aid workers said Banyamulenge Tutsi rebels battling the Zairean army cut a section of the highway between the eastern Zaire provincial towns of Bukavu and Uvira.
"The Banyamulenge rebels have taken up positions on both sides of the highway -- both up on the hills and on the plain -- so at the moment the road is impassable," one aid worker said.

"It is very difficult to get precise information at the moment. The only people who are able to circulate freely are the soldiers or the fighters," said the aid worker based in Bukavu, which is about 100 km (60 miles) north of Uvira.
Humanitarian workers in Uvira itself said many people had been killed and wounded in renewed fighting between the Zairean military and Banyamulenge rebels north of the town.
"There was heavy firing by automatic and light arms and mortars, leaving many dead and wounded," a senior aid worker told Reuters. He was unable to give precise casualty figures.

Tension in Bukavu rose dramatically following reports of intensifying fightging. Bukavu is the capital of South Kivu Province where a long-running struggle between Tutsi immigrants and indigenous Zaireans has sucked in the Zaire army.

There are hardly any Banyamulenge left in the province's main towns of Bukavu and Uvira. But tension hit boiling point two weeks ago when regional authorities ordered Tutsis living in villages on hills above Uvira to leave the province.
Zaire's central government tried to distance itself from the order but appeared powerless to protect an estimated 200,000 Tutsis who first settled some 200 years ago.
With the conflict looking likely to draw in the armies of neighbouring Rwanda and Burundi, both dominated by Tutsis, the U.N. dispatched envoy Ibrahim Fall to try and defuse tension.

"I am sent here as a special envoy of the United Nations Secretary General to try and find out as much as possible about the situation here on the ground," Fall told reporters in Bukavu. "I will be meeting with the local administration but also with as many other actors in the area as possible."
Asked if his brief was to stop the conflict drawing in the armies of Rwanda and Burundi, Fall said: "If I am able to, so much the better."
At least 28 civilians were killed and 17 wounded on Friday in fighting close to the Burundi border, aid workers said.

Elsewhere, military sources said Zairean soldiers were being resupplied with heavy weapons to respond to attacks by ethnic Tutsis, whom Zaire says have been sent by neighbouring Rwanda via Burundi to destablise its eastern region.

The flight of Banyamulenge from their homes in Zaire has created a new crisis in an area where 1.1 million Rwandan Hutu refugees are housed. The Hutu refugees fled, fearing retribution, after the 1994 genocide in Rwanda in which Hutus massacred an estimated one million Tutsis and moderate Hutus.

The presence of the Rwandan refugees in overcrowded camps in eastern Zaire has created security problems and has soured relations between Zaire and Rwanda, increasing Zairean hostility against the Banyamulenge.

Diplomats says the the violence in eastern Zaire has serious implications for the integrity of Zaire, a vast nation of 45 million people which has looked increasingly on the brink of political and economic collapse. Strongman President Mobutu Sese Seko, who has managed to hold it together during more than 30 years in power, is convalescing in Europe after cancer surgery.
